articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Issues ICC General Licenses, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. This action was part of a broader set of updates from OFAC.

In addition to the settlement, OFAC issued new General Licenses related to the International Criminal Court (ICC). These licenses aim to clarify permissible activities under U.S. sanctions programs concerning the ICC.
Furthermore, OFAC removed a designation related to Burma, indicating a change in sanctions policy or the resolution of issues that led to the initial designation.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new General License pertaining to Russia. This license authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Russia-related sanctions program.

The issuance of this General License suggests a specific carve-out or clarification for particular types of activities or entities, aiming to mitigate unintended consequences of the broader sanctions regime.
Parties involved in transactions with a nexus to Russia are advised to review the details of this new General License to ensure compliance and understand its scope.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Issues New Iran General License, and Amends Russia General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, targeting entities and individuals involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. This action is part of an intensified economic pressure campaign against Tehran, particularly targeting its oil trade and alleged sanctions-evasion networks.

Concurrently, OFAC issued a new General License related to Iran, which may permit certain humanitarian or other specific transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. This often accompanies broader sanctions to ensure essential activities can continue.

Additionally, an existing Russia-related General License was amended. Parties engaged in transactions under previous Russia-related authorizations should carefully review the revised terms, as the scope and conditions may have been adjusted.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes and Updates Designations, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designations removals and updates, indicating shifts in its sanctions lists. These changes can reflect evolving geopolitical situations or successful compliance efforts by previously designated entities.

In conjunction with these updates, OFAC published an Iran-related alert, likely warning about specific evasion tactics or emerging risks associated with transactions involving Iran. This alert aims to guide financial institutions and businesses in maintaining compliance.

Furthermore, an Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) was amended, providing updated guidance or clarification on existing sanctions policies concerning Iran. This helps stakeholders navigate the complexities of the sanctions regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under its counter-terrorism authorities. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations or engaging in terrorism-related activities globally.
These designations aim to disrupt financial networks and logistical support for terrorist groups, underscoring the U.S. commitment to combating global terrorism through economic sanctions.

Financial institutions and other regulated entities are advised to screen their transactions and customer bases against the updated Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List to ensure compliance with these new measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations, Publishes Determination and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) implemented new Iran-related designations and updates, further tightening sanctions against entities and individuals connected to the Iranian regime. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing activities.

Additionally, OFAC designated entities under its Transnational Criminal Organizations authority, targeting groups involved in illicit activities that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy.

A new Iran-related determination was published, alongside an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question, providing additional clarity and legal basis for the recent sanctions actions and offering updated guidance to the public.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Removes Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter-terrorism and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and activities that threaten international security.

In a separate move, OFAC removed several designations related to Belarus, counter narcotics efforts, and Libya. These removals suggest a re-evaluation of sanctions targets or a positive change in the behavior of the previously designated parties.
These simultaneous actions highlight OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, both imposing new restrictions where threats persist and lifting them where appropriate.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Narcotics, Counter Terrorism, Iran-Related, and Non-Proliferation Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a broad range of new designations, targeting entities and individuals under its counter narcotics, counter terrorism, Iran-related, and non-proliferation authorities. This comprehensive action underscores a multi-faceted approach to combating various threats to U.S. national security.

The Iran-related designations are part of an ongoing strategy to exert economic pressure on Tehran, while counter narcotics and counter terrorism designations aim to disrupt illicit networks globally. Non-proliferation designations target those involved in the spread of weapons of mass destruction.

These actions require financial institutions and other regulated entities to update their compliance programs and screening mechanisms to identify and block transactions involving the newly designated parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Regulatory Amendments, New Cuba Sanctions Regulations, and Amended FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a comprehensive regulatory package, including new Cuba Sanctions Regulations that took effect upon Federal Register publication on September 30, 2026.

These new regulations implement Executive Order (EO) 14404, issued on May 1, 2026, which focuses on imposing sanctions on those responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy.

The amendments to the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR) restrict indirect dealings with Cuba Restricted List entities, eliminate the U-turn authorization, and remove group people-to-people and professional-meeting travel authorizations. OFAC also issued new and amended Cuba-related Frequently Asked Questions and a Cuba-related OFAC Alert to provide further guidance.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / The National Law Review

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Venezuela General Licenses

The revisions to these General Licenses may impact various sectors, including oil, gas, and humanitarian aid, by adjusting the scope of permissible activities or the conditions under which they can be conducted. Companies operating under Venezuela authorizations should confirm they are relying on the current version of each license.

Stakeholders are advised to carefully review the updated licenses to understand any new restrictions or expanded authorizations, ensuring continued compliance with U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela.

articles.headline: Fed Governor Waller Signals Further Rate Hikes Amid Persistent Inflation Concerns
body: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher J. Waller indicated a pivot towards further monetary policy tightening, citing persistent price pressures and shifting economic risks. His remarks, prepared for the Istanbul Economic Forum on October 8, highlighted the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) September decision to raise the benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to a range of 3.75% to 4%.

This September hike ended a nine-month pause and reversed a sequence of late-2025 rate cuts. Waller attributed the stalled progress toward the Fed's 2% inflation target to a confluence of pressures, including stubborn energy costs tied to the Iran war, rising tech prices driven by the AI buildout, and looming trade tariffs.

Consumer confidence is slipping, and household inflation expectations are climbing, with the New York Fed's September Survey of Consumer Expectations showing a median one-year-ahead inflation expectation jumping 0.3% to 3.9%, the highest level in three years. Waller emphasized that while labor-market stability provides room to maneuver, policymakers are prepared for further tightening if inflation fails to abate.

articles.headline: Upcoming CPI Report Expected to Show Accelerated Headline Inflation
body: All eyes are on the upcoming U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation data, slated for release on October 14. Consensus forecasts anticipate an acceleration in headline inflation, largely driven by higher energy prices.

While the monthly core measure for September is expected to be tame at 0.2% (down from 0.3% in August), headline inflation is projected to jump from 0.4% to 0.6%. This would place the annual inflation measures at 2.5% and 3.6%, respectively.

A hotter-than-consensus CPI print could disrupt expectations of an October pause in interest rate hikes and fuel further fixed-income volatility, as evidence already points to some leakage of interest-rate risk into credit risk. Producer Price Index (PPI) data is also expected to show a jump in monthly measures for both core and headline producer prices.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank (AENB) for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC determined that AENB failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations. Deficiencies included inadequate resources, staff lacking sufficient expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and insufficient BSA/AML training.

The bank also failed to tailor its BSA/AML risk assessment to its business activities, focusing too narrowly on demand deposit accounts while neglecting the risks in its more dominant credit and charge card products. These failures led to systemic breakdowns in suspicious activity monitoring and reporting, resulting in a failure to timely identify and report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Traders Union

articles.headline: BIS Adds Over Three Dozen Entities to Entity List, Citing National Security and Foreign Policy Concerns
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced the addition of more than three dozen companies to its Entity List, effective immediately. This marks the second round of restrictions imposed by the United States in as many weeks.

The Entity List identifies parties believed to be involved in, or posing a significant risk of becoming involved in, activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States. These entities are now subject to restrictive licensing requirements and policies.

Of the 37 entities added, most (28) are from China, with others from Belarus, Burma, Pakistan, Russia, and Taiwan. BIS cited support for Chinese military modernization, sanctioned parties in Iran, ballistic missile and unsafeguarded nuclear activities, support for Russia's military, and human rights violations in China and Burma as reasons for the designations.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Legal 500

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
